right_of_way.stations_doc: Each ribbon is a run of stations [e_west, n_west, e_east, n_east] across it, every 5 m along it; `made_ground` is T-2479's strip between the east verge and the lake edge's crest.
right_of_way.note: Where the cinders stop and the weeds begin is not drawn on either sheet: the edges are the outermost tracks plus the spec's margins, smoothed. RECONSTRUCTED (L-ic-tracks-2478).

lake_edge.stations_doc: `face` runs from the toe under the water to the crest, as stations [e_lake, n_lake, e_land, n_land] every 5 m along the shore; `crest` is the cap timber's line. The made ground between the crest and the east verge is right_of_way.made_ground.
lake_edge.note: The face, its crest and the waterline are the committed heightfield's (terrain_spec ic_row_embankment); what the face is made of, the cap and the piles are not read off any source. RECONSTRUCTED (L-ic-lake-edge-2479).

gauge_note: Standard gauge, 4 ft 8 1/2 in, between the rails' inner faces. The Illinois Central and the Michigan Central ran standard gauge by 1904 (the IC's southern lines were converted in 1881). Inferred: the gauge of the period's trunk lines, not read off this track.

rail.note: The American Society of Civil Engineers' 1893 section at 85 lb per yard (5 3/16 in high and wide at the base, a 2 9/16 in head, a 9/16 in web): the common trunk-line rail of the years either side of 1904. Which weight these tracks carried is not read; a heavier section is about a centimetre taller. RECONSTRUCTED.

ties.note: Hewn or sawn crossties 8 ft long, 7 x 9 in, about eighteen to a 30-ft rail: the dimensions the period's railway engineering texts give for main track. George Glessner's photograph looking north from 18th Street (Prairie library st-ghm-george-glessner-ic-train-18th) shows the ties as a close ladder with the ballast filled nearly to their tops, so they stand only a few centimetres proud of it. Spacing, size and the irregularity of a hand-laid track are ours. RECONSTRUCTED.

ballast.note: Both George Glessner photographs of the tracks at 18th Street (st-ghm-george-glessner-ic-train-18th, a18-gh-ic-train-foot-of-18th-c1888) show a dark, fine, earthy bed filled up round the ties and the same dark ground trodden flat between the tracks: locomotive cinders, the ballast every Chicago railway of the period had in quantity. No lawn and no pale broken stone shows in either. INFERRED for what the photographs show; the bed's width, the grain and colour of the maps are ours (RECONSTRUCTED).

verges.note: Grass and weeds along the right-of-way's edges and a few in the cinders between the tracks: what grows on a railway's disturbed ground in a Chicago July. No photograph read shows the verge at this reach in summer (both Glessner views are winter or bare). The species mix, its height and density are ours. RECONSTRUCTED.

face.note: The embankment's lakeward face, from about 1.5 m lakeward of the waterline, under the water, to the crest, at the heightfield's 1 in 1.5. No beach: the 1886 and 1911 maps draw the water against the railway's edge and the 1891 atlas its breakwater offshore (docs/RESEARCH/ic_lakefront_1904.md). What the face was made of at this reach is not read off any source; it is drawn as dumped quarry stone, the protection a railway laid along a lake embankment in the period, buff-grey Lemont-Joliet limestone, darker and greener where the water keeps it wet. RECONSTRUCTED.

stones.note: Single blocks stood on the face near the eye, angular, 0.45 to 1.1 m across, seated on their flat undersides and sunk among the rest. Their size, shape, number and stone are ours. RECONSTRUCTED.

cap.note: A 12 x 12 in timber along the crest, standing a few centimetres proud of the made ground, capping the piles that hold the head of the stone: the way the period built a timber-and-stone lake edge. Not read off this reach. RECONSTRUCTED.

piles.note: Round timber piles under the cap, one every 10 ft, the spacing the railway's 1852 breakwater cribs were held at; seen only where the stone leaves them bare. RECONSTRUCTED.

made_ground.note: Sanborn 1911 sheet 28 draws about 16 m of ground between the easternmost track and the water at 18th Street, the made ground L287 moves the 1911 edge east by: filled ground behind the railway's edge. That it is there is INFERRED from the sheet; what it was made of (cinders, sand and builders' fill, with weeds) and how it looked are RECONSTRUCTED.
